title: Consensus with Raft
goal: By the end, you can explain how Raft keeps the same list of payments on five computers through crashes and lost messages: how they elect a leader, how the leader copies each payment and decides it's saved, why a new leader never loses a saved one, and how to read from the group and change its members safely.
opening:
Picture a café at lunchtime. You tap your card, and the screen says Approved. Behind that word, the payments app saved your payment on five computers, in case one breaks. One of them, the leader, takes each payment and copies it to the others.

Then the leader's network cable comes loose. The other four pick a new leader and carry on. The old one keeps taking payments it can't copy anywhere. When the cable goes back in, it holds more payments than any other.

The easy fix is to keep the longest list, since throwing payments away sounds like the worst thing a payments app could do. But none of the old leader's extra payments was approved, and its list lacks payments whose customers saw Approved.

Total order broadcast and the many faces of consensus kept copies identical with a log, and Paxos agreed on one entry of it. In this lesson, we'll build the whole log with Raft, and cut its leader off to see which list wins. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Five computers keep the payments app's list of payments. The leader adds a new payment to its own list and sends it to the other four. Two of them reply that they've saved it; the other two haven't answered yet. When may the leader tell the card reader Approved?
options: Now: the leader and the two that replied make three of five, more than half
Only once all four of the others have saved it
As soon as the leader has saved it on its own disk
After its next check that all five computers are still running
warmup.why: Raft counts a payment as saved, which it calls committed, once more than half of the computers hold it, the leader included: three of five here. Any future leader needs votes from three computers too, and any two groups of three out of five share at least one computer. That shared computer holds the payment, and it votes only for a candidate that holds it as well (the fourth section shows how). Waiting for all four would let one slow computer hold up every payment. The leader's own disk survives a restart, but not the loss of that one machine.

sections.h: From one decision to a list of them: Raft's picture
sections.body:
The payments app keeps every card payment in a log: a numbered list of commands that only ever grows at the end. Entry 1 might be "card 4242 pays the café 4.50", entry 2 a refund, entry 3 the next payment. Any copy that runs the same commands in the same order ends with the same balances. So to survive a broken machine, we keep the log on several computers, which Raft calls servers. Every server must hold the same entry in each numbered slot.

That's harder than it sounds, because servers crash and messages get lost or arrive late. Getting servers to agree in spite of that is called consensus. Total order broadcast and the many faces of consensus agreed on one value with Paxos. The server that wants a value chosen, the proposer, asks a majority of servers (more than half: three of five) to promise to ignore older proposals. Then it asks them to accept its value: two round trips, each a message there and an answer back. Any two majorities of five share a server, so once a value is chosen, every later proposer meets a server that knows it. For a whole log there's a shortcut, Multi-Paxos: a leader that stays in charge makes the promise round once, then pays one round trip per entry.

That leaves everything around the shortcut open. Who becomes leader, and when? How does a new leader learn which slots the last one left half-decided? How does a crashed server catch up, and how do servers join or leave? The Paxos papers leave those to whoever builds it.

Raft, published by Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout in 2014, answers all of them, and was designed to be easy to understand. It keeps Multi-Paxos's shape: one leader at a time, a majority for every decision, one round trip per write. Then it adds rules that make the rest mechanical. Time is cut into numbered terms, with at most one leader each. Only the leader adds to the log, and entries flow one way, from the leader to its followers. And only a server whose log already holds every saved entry can win an election, so a new leader never has holes to fill.

The figure is Raft's picture, and the rest of the lesson adds to it. Each small box is an entry, labelled with its term (t1, t2). The leader copies its log to the followers. An entry is **committed**, Raft's word for safely saved, once a majority stores it. Every server then runs the committed entries, in log order, against its own copy of the data, which Raft calls the state machine: here, the table of balances. Five servers survive two failures, and three survive one. In general, 2f + 1 servers survive f failures.

Before anything can be copied, somebody has to lead. Next, we'll hold the election.

aside.title: Wouldn't four servers be safer than three?
aside.body: It feels that way, but no. A majority of four is three, so four servers survive one failure, exactly like three, and every write waits for one more copy. Where the servers stand matters as much as how many there are. Three servers split two and one across two buildings lose their majority whenever the building with two loses power. So real groups run three or five servers, spread over three separate places, so that losing any one place leaves a majority. Going beyond five mostly makes each write slower, because it waits for more copies.

sections.h: Choosing a leader: terms, votes and random timers
sections.body:
Picture a club that keeps a minutes book. Each period of office has one chair, chosen by a vote. If the chair stops turning up, a member calls an election, and the next period begins. Raft runs its servers the same way: the chair is the leader, the period of office is a **term**, and the minutes book is the log.

Every server is a follower, a candidate or a leader, and all start as followers. The leader sends each follower a message every so often, every 50 ms in the lab's simulator. Most carry new entries; when there's nothing to copy, an empty one, called a heartbeat, says "I'm still here". A follower that hears nothing for a while, its election timeout, decides the leader is gone and starts an election.

Terms are numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on, and every message carries the sender's term. A server that sees a higher term than its own takes that number and becomes a follower. A message with a lower term is refused. So a leader that was cut off learns it has been replaced from the first reply it gets, and nobody acts on its old messages.

An election runs like this. The follower adds one to its term, becomes a candidate, votes for itself, and asks every other server for its vote with a message called RequestVote. A server grants at most one vote per term, to the first candidate that asks (a later section adds one condition). It writes the vote to disk before it answers, so a crash and restart can't make it vote twice. A candidate with votes from a majority becomes leader and sends heartbeats at once, which resets everyone's timer. Two leaders in one term would need two majorities with no server in common, and five servers can't form those.

What if two followers time out together? Both become candidates in the same term, each votes for itself, and the votes split, two and two, with the fifth lost or late. Nobody has a majority, so both time out and retry in a higher term, perhaps forever. So Raft draws each timeout at random, from 150 to 300 ms in the paper. One server usually times out well before the others and collects its votes before anyone else wakes up.

The paper measured this on five servers. With no randomness, split votes kept the group without a leader for more than 10 seconds. With only 5 ms of randomness, the median time without a leader (the middle value of many runs) fell to 287 ms. With 50 ms, the worst of 1,000 trials took 513 ms. Shorter timeouts elect faster: with 12 to 24 ms, a new leader was in place after 35 ms on average.

Timeouts can't shrink forever, though. A round of messages to every server and back, disk writes included, takes 0.5 to 20 ms in the paper's estimate. The timeout must be many of those, or followers start elections against a healthy leader whose heartbeat was merely slow. It must also be tiny next to the months between server failures, since after a crash there's no leader for about one timeout. That puts it between 10 and 500 ms. etcd, a small database built on Raft, defaults to a 100 ms heartbeat and a 1,000 ms election timeout.

The club picture breaks in one place. Members in a room can see who's there. A server can't tell a dead leader from a slow network, so every rule runs on timers and term numbers.

The Try it runs both cases in the lab's simulator. Once a leader has won, it can copy payments. Next, we'll see how.

sections.h: Copying the log: AppendEntries and the check that keeps every copy equal
sections.body:
A card reader sends the leader a payment. The leader adds it to the end of its log as an entry: the command plus the leader's current term. Its place is the next free index, the entry's number in the log. Then the leader sends each follower a message called AppendEntries. It carries the new entries and two numbers about the entry right before them: that entry's index, `prevLogIndex`, and its term, `prevLogTerm`. A follower accepts only if its own log has an entry at that index with that term. If it does, it deletes any of its own entries from that point on that disagree with the new ones, and adds the ones it lacks.

Why check only one entry? Picture two copies of the club's minutes, compared at the end of every meeting. If both agree on the last line, and every earlier comparison passed, the two copies match all the way up. Raft argues the same way. An empty log matches the start of any log, and each accepted AppendEntries extends a matching start with matching entries. So if two logs hold an entry with the same index and term, they hold the same command there and the same entries before it. Raft calls this the Log Matching Property: one (index, term) pair vouches for the whole history before it.

When the check fails, the follower's log differs somewhere earlier. It may have missed entries while it was down, or hold entries from an old leader that were never committed. The leader keeps a `nextIndex` for each follower, the next entry to send it. On a refusal, it moves `nextIndex` back by one and tries again, until the two logs agree. The follower then drops its entries from the point where the logs differ, and takes the leader's. The leader never deletes anything from its own log. Lost messages need no special care: the next heartbeat resends everything from `nextIndex`.

The leader also keeps a `matchIndex` for each follower: how far that follower's log is known to match its own. Once a majority holds an entry, counting the leader, the entry is committed. The leader applies it to its state machine and answers the card reader. Followers learn the new commit point from a field called `leaderCommit` in the next AppendEntries, and apply the entry too.

So a write costs one round trip to the fastest half of the followers, and one slow follower slows nobody down. One more cost sits on that path. A server must force each entry onto its disk before it says it has it. It uses `fsync`, the call from Write-ahead logging and crash recovery that makes the operating system copy data from memory onto the disk. "I have it" has to survive a power cut.

In the Try it, 16 of 152 messages are lost, and every payment still commits, some a few dozen milliseconds late. Two followers crash, and the leader carries on with the three servers left. When a third crashes, the leader can't reach a majority, and the next payment waits until a crashed follower comes back.

**A payment is saved when a majority has it on disk, and not before.** Next, we'll crash the leader and see whether that promise holds.

sections.h: When the leader crashes: why the new one already has every saved payment
sections.body:
Leaders crash, and the server that takes over may have missed entries. If a server missing a committed entry could win, it would force its log onto the others and delete a payment whose customer saw Approved. Raft closes that hole in the vote.

RequestVote carries the index and term of the candidate's last log entry. A voter refuses any candidate whose log is less up to date than its own. Which log is more up to date? The one whose last entry has the higher term. If the last terms are equal, the longer log wins. So length alone counts for little: a long log that ends in an old term loses to a shorter one that ends in a newer term. That's the opening's trap, answered.

Now put the majorities together. A committed entry is on a majority of servers. A winner needs votes from a majority. Any two majorities share at least one server, and that server votes only for a candidate whose log holds everything its own does. So every new leader already has every committed entry.

One trap is left, shown in Figure 8 of the paper. A new leader finds an entry from an earlier term in its log, and a majority holds it. Is it committed? Not necessarily. A server whose last entry has a newer term could still win an election and overwrite it. So a Raft leader counts copies only for entries of its own term. Older entries become committed when an entry of the current term after them does. That's why the lab's leaders add a no-op, an entry that does nothing, the moment they win. It gives them something of their own term to commit at once, and everything before it commits with it.

Not every entry survives a crash, and that's by design. An entry the old leader couldn't copy to a majority was never committed, so its card reader never got an answer, and a new leader may replace it. The card reader gives up waiting and sends the payment again. The paper's advice is to give every command a unique serial number, so the state machine can spot a repeat and not apply it twice. Payment systems call this an idempotency key: a label that makes sending a request twice the same as sending it once.

The stepper follows one payment through a leader crash. In the Try it, a cut-off leader keeps accepting a payment it can never commit, until a higher term makes it throw the entry away.

This machinery runs inside etcd, and inside CockroachDB, a database spread over many machines. CockroachDB runs one Raft group, a set of servers running Raft together, for each slice of its data.

Next, we'll look at what real systems add on top: safe reads, new members, and Kafka's version.

With its own vote, S3 has 4 of 5, more than the 3 it needs: **S3 leads term 1**. It adds a no-op entry of its own term (the section says why) and starts sending AppendEntries every 50 ms.

sections.h: Reading safely, changing the members, and Kafka's version of Raft
sections.body:
In the last Try it, the cut-off n2 still believed it led term 1 while n1 committed pay-3. Gaps like that catch out real systems in three places outside the core rules.

The first is reads. A leader holds every committed entry, so it's tempting to answer a balance check from its own copy without asking anyone. But a leader can be replaced without knowing it, like n2. A read from n2 would miss pay-3 after other readers had already seen it. That breaks the rule from Linearizability: one copy, one timeline. Once anyone has seen a new value, no later read may return an older one.

Sending every read through the log works, but then a read costs as much as a write. The paper gives two cheaper ways. With **ReadIndex**, the leader notes its commit index and confirms it still leads, with one round of heartbeats to a majority. Once it has applied up to that index, it answers: one round trip, no disk write. (A new leader must commit its no-op first, or it doesn't know its own commit index.) With a lease, a promise that lasts a fixed time, the leader answers alone, with no round trip at all. It relies on the followers' promise not to start an election until a timeout after they last heard from it. That's safe only if the servers' clocks run at nearly the same rate and the leader never freezes. Clocks you can't trust and Process pauses, in the Faults, time and truth track, showed that both can fail. etcd serves its default reads with ReadIndex.

The second is changing the members. Servers switch to a new member list at different moments, so for a while some count majorities of the old list and some of the new one. Going from three servers straight to five lets two old servers and three new ones each form a majority, and elect two leaders in one term. The paper's answer is joint consensus: a changeover entry during which every decision needs a majority of both lists. Ongaro's thesis later offered a simpler rule: change one server at a time. Any majority of n servers shares a server with any majority of n + 1 or n - 1.

In July 2015, Ongaro announced on the Raft mailing list that this alone is unsafe. From four servers, a term-1 leader added S5, reached only S5 and went offline. A term-2 leader then removed S1 and committed that on S2 and S3. Then S1 won term 3 with votes from S1, S4 and S5, and overwrote the committed entry. The fix is one rule: a leader may not start a membership change until it has committed an entry of its own term, its no-op.

The third is Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages for other programs. Since Kafka 4.0 (March 2025), the cluster's own records live in a Raft log called `__cluster_metadata`, kept by three or five controllers, servers whose job is this log. Those records say, for example, which topics (named logs of messages) exist and which computer leads each. KRaft, Kafka's Raft, turns the messages around: followers pull. Each asks the leader for anything after its last entry, and that request doubles as the heartbeat. Kafka calls a term an epoch, and a new leader moves its commit point only once an entry of its own epoch is on a majority: Figure 8's rule again.

The lab puts the core of these rules together, in a simulator you can break on purpose.

a.label: PostgreSQL
a.title: primary + standbys
a.src:
synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 2 (s1, s2, s3)'

b.label: Raft
b.title: five servers
b.src:

the leader is elected by majority vote

compare.note: Both wait for several copies before a commit counts, so neither loses a confirmed write when one machine dies. (A standby is PostgreSQL's name for a copy that follows the primary, the one copy that takes writes.) The difference is who decides which machine is in charge. PostgreSQL leaves it to a person or an outside tool, and that tool needs a consensus store of its own, or it could end up with two primaries. Raft decides inside the protocol, and its vote rule makes sure the new leader already holds every committed entry.

lab.title: Build the core of Raft in a simulator
steps: Read `Messages.kt`, the messages the servers send each other. Then read the half of `RaftNode.kt` below the "provided" line, which is written for you: `receive` (it moves to a higher term for you), `tick`, `startElection` and `becomeLeader`. `Cluster.kt` runs five servers on a pretend network and checks Raft's safety rules every simulated millisecond. Run the tests once: all 14 fail.
Write `handleRequestVote`, a server's answer to a request for its vote. The first two tests pass.

Write `handleAppendEntries`: the term check, the check on the entry before the new ones, cutting a conflicting tail, adding the new entries, and the follower's commit index. Four more tests pass: the older-term test and the three follower tests.
Write `handleAppendReply` and `advanceCommitIndex`, the leader's side. The three leader tests pass, including the Figure 8 test.

Run all 14. The five cluster tests need all four handlers: they elect leaders, lose 10% to 15% of messages, crash and restart servers, and cut one off the network. If one fails, print `c.events` in the test to read its timeline.
hints: In `handleAppendEntries`, check `req.prevLogIndex > lastLogIndex` before you call `termAt(req.prevLogIndex)`, or you read past the end of the log.

Never delete entries that match. An old AppendEntries can arrive late, after a newer one, carrying fewer entries; it must leave the newer entries in place. Only a different term at the same index cuts the log.
The follower's commit index is `maxOf(commitIndex, minOf(req.leaderCommit, req.prevLogIndex + req.entries.size))`. It follows the leader, never passes what this request proved, and never goes back.

In `advanceCommitIndex`, walk from `lastLogIndex` down to `commitIndex + 1`, and stop at the first entry that isn't from `currentTerm`. Count the servers with `matchIndex[i] >= n`. The leader's own entry is `matchIndex[id]`, which `propose` keeps up to date.

drill.title: Write a follower's AppendEntries handler from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. From memory, write `handleAppendEntries(req)` for a follower whose `receive` has already taken on any higher term. Include the term check, the check on `prevLogIndex` and `prevLogTerm`, the loop that keeps matching entries and cuts at the first conflict, and the commit index. Logs are numbered from 1, and `termAt(0)` is 0.

recap: Paxos agrees on one value, and a database needs a log of them, the same on every server. Raft gets there with one leader per numbered term, a log that flows one way, and an election rule.

A follower that hears no leader for a random timeout (150 to 300 ms in the paper, 1,000 ms by default in etcd) starts an election in a new term, and each server votes once per term. Without the randomness, split votes kept a group leaderless for more than 10 seconds.
AppendEntries carries the index and term of the entry before the new ones, and a follower accepts only if its log has that entry. So two logs that share one (index, term) pair match up to there.

An entry is committed once a majority has it on disk, and a leader counts copies only for entries of its own term (Figure 8). Voters refuse candidates whose logs are less up to date, so every new leader holds every committed entry.

A leader's read is safe only after a heartbeat round to a majority (ReadIndex) or inside a clock-based lease. Members change one server at a time, and only after the new leader has committed its no-op.

The limit: every write waits for a majority, so a group that loses its majority stops taking writes, and more servers make each write slower, not faster. A payment that wasn't committed can vanish in a crash, so clients send it again with an idempotency key.
closing:
We started with a cut-off leader holding the longest list of payments, and the urge to keep it. Raft keeps the other list. A payment counts only once a majority has it on disk. Votes go only to logs that hold every such payment, and the old leader's extra entries, which nobody was promised, are dropped.

Open raft.github.io, where an animation runs five servers in your browser. Stop the leader and watch which follower's timer runs out first. Then stop two more followers, and see whether the new leader can still commit anything.

Next, we'll meet the small services built on this, such as etcd and ZooKeeper, and ask why so many systems borrow their agreement instead of building it.

quiz.q: A Raft leader answers reads from its own copy of the data without asking anyone. A network fault cuts it off, the other four servers elect a new leader, and the new leader commits a refund that a second customer then reads. A third customer now reads from the old leader. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: a Raft leader holds every committed entry, so its reads are always current
The read can miss the refund that someone else already saw, which breaks linearizability. With ReadIndex, the old leader would have checked with a majority first and found it had been replaced
The read waits until the network fault is fixed
The old leader can't answer at all, because it sees the new leader's higher term
quiz.why: A leader holds every entry committed before its term began, not entries committed after it was replaced. The old leader hasn't heard the higher term yet, so it doesn't know it has missed anything, and it answers with data older than what the second customer saw. Linearizability: one copy, one timeline calls that history wrong: once anyone has seen the refund, no later read may miss it. That's why the first option fails. ReadIndex needs a heartbeat round with a majority before answering, and a cut-off leader can't complete one. The last option fails because the old leader learns the higher term only when a message reaches it.

quiz.q: A candidate's log ends at index 8, term 2. A voter's log ends at index 5, term 3. Neither has voted in the current term. Does the voter grant its vote?
options: Yes: the candidate's log is longer
Yes: the voter hasn't voted in this term
No: the voter's last entry has a higher term, so its log is more up to date
Only if the candidate's term is higher than 3
quiz.why: Raft compares the terms of the last entries first, and compares lengths only when those are equal. The voter's term-3 entry may be committed, and a leader whose log ends in term 2 doesn't have it and could overwrite it. A long log of old-term entries is worth less than one entry from a newer term, which is the opening's trap: the longest list isn't the safest one. Not having voted yet is necessary, but it isn't enough.

quiz.q: The leader of term 4 finds an entry from term 2 at index 6 of its log. Three of the five servers store it. May the leader mark index 6 committed now?
options: Yes: a majority has it
No: it must first get an entry from term 4 onto a majority, and index 6 is committed along with it
No: a new leader always deletes entries from old terms
Only once all five servers store it
quiz.why: This is Figure 8 of the Raft paper. An old-term entry on a majority can still be overwritten, because a server whose last entry has a newer term could win an election. So a leader commits only entries of its own term by counting copies, and once one of those is on a majority, everything before it is committed too. The first option is tempting because it's the rule for entries of the current term. New leaders keep old entries; they don't delete them.

quiz.q: A network fault cuts the leader off from the other four servers. For ten seconds a card reader keeps sending it payments, and the leader adds each one to its log. What happens to those payments?
options: They're committed when the network heals, because the leader logged them first
They're never committed: the leader can't reach a majority, the card reader gets no answer, and the new leader's log replaces them
They're committed at once, because a leader commits its own entries
Raft rejects them, because a cut-off leader knows it has lost its majority
quiz.why: Without copies on a majority nothing commits, so the card reader never gets an OK and gives up waiting. Meanwhile the other four elect a leader in a higher term. When the network heals, the old leader sees the higher term and becomes a follower, and its uncommitted entries conflict with the new leader's log and are dropped. The last option is tempting, but the old leader doesn't know it's cut off; it only sees no replies. That's why the card reader must send each payment again, with an idempotency key so the card isn't charged twice.

quiz.q: From Write-ahead logging and crash recovery: a follower replies that it has stored an entry before forcing it to disk, then loses power. Why does that break Raft?
options: It doesn't: the leader still has the entry
The leader counted that follower toward the majority, so a committed entry may now be on fewer than a majority, and a leader elected without it could overwrite it
The follower will vote twice in the same term
AppendEntries will fail forever on that follower
quiz.why: Committed means on the disks of a majority. If one of the three copies vanishes in the power cut, only two servers hold the entry. A new leader can then win with votes from servers that lack it and replace it, after a customer was told the payment is saved. That's the write-ahead log's rule again: say it's stored only after it's forced to disk. The first option fails because the leader alone isn't a majority, and it can crash too. A server's vote must reach its disk before it answers, for the same reason.

flashcards.front: How does a Raft leader answer a read safely without adding it to the log (ReadIndex)?
flashcards.back: It notes its commit index, confirms it still leads with one round of heartbeats to a majority, waits until it has applied up to that index, then answers. One round trip, no disk write.

flashcards.front: What went wrong with changing Raft's members one server at a time (2015)?
flashcards.back: Two changes, started from the same four servers by different leaders, gave member lists whose majorities don't overlap. Fix: a leader commits an entry of its own term before any change.

flashcards.front: Why are election timeouts random, and how much does it matter?
flashcards.back: So one follower usually times out first and wins before the others start. In the paper, no randomness meant more than 10 s of split votes; 5 ms of randomness gave a 287 ms median.

flashcards.front: What does a follower check before it accepts AppendEntries?
flashcards.back: That its log has an entry at `prevLogIndex` with term `prevLogTerm`. If not, it refuses, and the leader steps `nextIndex` back by one and tries again.

flashcards.front: When does a Raft leader commit an entry?
flashcards.back: When a majority stores it and it's from the leader's current term. Earlier entries commit along with it.

flashcards.front: Which candidates does a server refuse to vote for?
flashcards.back: Any whose log is less up to date: an older last term, or the same last term and a shorter log. And any second candidate in a term it has already voted in.

flashcards.front: What happens to an entry the old leader never got onto a majority?
flashcards.back: It was never committed, and the new leader's log may replace it. Its client got no OK and must send it again, ideally with an idempotency key.

terms.plain: Servers that can crash and lose messages agreeing on one value, or on one order of log entries.
More than half of the servers, such as 3 of 5. Any two majorities share at least one server.
Raft's numbered period of leadership. Each one starts with an election and has at most one leader.
How long a follower waits without hearing from a leader before it starts an election. It's random, 150 to 300 ms in the paper.
The leader's message that copies log entries to a follower. An empty one is a heartbeat.
If two logs have an entry with the same index and term, they're identical up to that entry.
An entry stored on a majority of servers. It will never be lost, and every server applies it in order.
A safe read: the leader confirms with a majority that it still leads, then answers once it has applied up to its commit index.

explain_back.prompt: The leader of a five-server Raft group crashes right after it committed a payment that only two followers had stored. Using the vote rule, explain why the payment can't be lost.
explain_back.answer: The payment is committed, so it's on three servers: the old leader and two followers. To become the new leader, a candidate needs votes from three of the five servers. The old leader is down, so any three of the four live servers include at least one of the two followers that hold the payment. A voter refuses a candidate whose log is less up to date than its own, comparing the term of the last entry first and the length second. So a follower holding the payment votes only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date, which means a log that also holds the payment. Whoever wins already has it, and since a leader never deletes its own entries, it copies the payment to the others instead of overwriting it.

deeper.body:
**Log compaction.** A log can't grow forever. Each server saves a snapshot of its state machine to disk and throws away the log up to that point (section 7 of the paper). A follower that falls too far behind gets the leader's snapshot instead of the entries, through a third message, InstallSnapshot.

**PreVote and CheckQuorum.** A server cut off by a flaky link keeps timing out and raising its term. When it reconnects, its high term forces a healthy leader to step down. With PreVote, a candidate first asks whether it could win before it raises its term. With CheckQuorum, a leader steps down by itself when it stops hearing from a majority. Ongaro's thesis describes both, and the etcd-io/raft library implements them. The next lesson shows a partial network fault that left a three-server etcd group stuck in tied elections.

**Many Raft groups.** One Raft group has one leader and one log, which limits how fast it can take writes. CockroachDB and TiKV (a key-value store built the same way) split their keys into ranges and run one Raft group per range, thousands per cluster, so the leaders spread over many machines. Distributed SQL: Spanner, CockroachDB and Aurora DSQL builds a database out of exactly that.

**Kafka's pull-based Raft in more detail.** A KRaft follower's Fetch request carries its log end offset and the epoch of its last entry. When the logs have parted, the leader answers with a `DivergingEpoch` that tells the follower where to cut its log. A voter that gets no successful answer to its fetches within its timeout starts an election. Kafka's high watermark is Raft's commit index, and a new leader writes a leader-change record in its own epoch before it moves the high watermark. Because followers pull, every broker can follow the metadata log as an observer that never votes, the way Kafka followers already copy partitions. KIP-595 is the design document.

**Raft in the wild.** The 2015 membership bug was found by two students at Carnegie Mellon University while they wrote Raft out as a precise mathematical model. In the Raft paper's study, 33 of 43 students scored better on a Raft quiz than on a Paxos one. Before Raft, every team that built Multi-Paxos filled in the missing pieces on its own; Google's "Paxos Made Live" (2007) describes what that took for its lock service, Chubby. Today etcd, CockroachDB and TiKV run the etcd-io/raft library, and Consul (another coordination store) runs HashiCorp's. The library in etcd 3.7 hardened ReadIndex against stale reads. Every proof assumes that what a server acknowledged is on its disk. Jepsen, a project that tests databases by breaking them on purpose, analysed NATS JetStream, a messaging system, in 2025. JetStream uses Raft but by default flushes to disk only every two minutes while acknowledging at once, and it lost 131,418 of 930,005 acknowledged messages in a simulated power failure: the last quiz question, at scale. DynamoDB's partitions use Multi-Paxos instead, as the Partitioning track's DynamoDB lesson shows.
